description: Sports boycotts, sanctions and divestment — global pressure squeezes apartheid's economy.
content_html:
The International Response to Apartheid

Resistance to apartheid was not confined to South Africa. From the early 1960s, an international movement grew to isolate the apartheid regime through boycotts, sanctions and public protest. The Anti-Apartheid Movement (AAM) was founded in Britain in 1959, initially as a small activist group. By the 1980s it had become a mass movement with significant political influence.

Trevor Huddleston, an Anglican priest who had lived and worked in Sophiatown (a vibrant mixed-race area of Johannesburg that was demolished under the Group Areas Act), was a founding figure of the British AAM. His memoir Naught for Your Comfort (1956) had introduced many British readers to the reality of apartheid.

Key Fact

Three major forms of international pressure combined: sports isolation (South Africa excluded from the Olympics from 1964; Gleneagles Agreement 1977 on Commonwealth sports), economic sanctions (US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act 1986; Chase Manhattan refused to roll over loans 1985) and diplomatic isolation (expelled from the Commonwealth 1961; UN mandatory arms embargo 1977).

Sports Isolation

Sport was among the most publicly visible fronts of the isolation campaign. South Africa was excluded from the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and banned from all subsequent Games until 1992. In 1970 the International Cricket Conference expelled South Africa. The Gleneagles Agreement (1977) committed Commonwealth governments to discouraging sporting contact with South Africa. When rebel cricket and rugby tours were organised in defiance of the boycott, they provoked significant protests.

For many white South Africans, the sports boycott was among the most psychologically damaging forms of isolation — South Africa had strong sporting traditions and international competition mattered to white identity. Apartheid supporters argued the boycott was “politics in sport”; anti-apartheid campaigners replied that apartheid itself had already politicised sport by enforcing racial selection policies.

Economic pressure grew through the 1980s. In 1985, the Chase Manhattan Bank refused to roll over South Africa’s short-term loans — a dramatic signal that international financial confidence in the regime was collapsing. Other banks followed. The South African government declared a debt moratorium in September 1985.

In 1986, the United States Congress passed the Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act, imposing sweeping economic sanctions. President Reagan vetoed the bill on “constructive engagement” grounds, but Congress overrode his veto — a rare and significant act. Universities, pension funds and corporations across the US and Europe were pressured by campaign groups to divest from companies doing business in South Africa.

Oliver Tambo and Desmond Tutu

Oliver Tambo’s work in exile was central to the international campaign. He lobbied the United Nations, the Organisation of African Unity and sympathetic governments. The ANC under his leadership maintained MK training camps and built alliances with the Soviet Union, Sweden and other states that provided financial and logistical support.

Desmond Tutu, Archbishop of Cape Town from 1986 and Nobel Peace Prize winner (1984), was one of the most prominent internal voices calling for sanctions. He argued that economic pressure was the only non-violent alternative to escalating violence inside South Africa.

Key Fact

Reagan and Thatcher both opposed comprehensive sanctions, arguing that “constructive engagement” — maintaining economic ties — would encourage reform more effectively. Critics (including Tutu and the ANC) argued this was a justification for protecting Western economic interests and that it gave the regime legitimacy it did not deserve.

South Africa had been expelled from the Commonwealth in 1961. In 1977, following Biko’s death and the Soweto uprising, the United Nations Security Council passed Resolution 418 — a mandatory arms embargo that required all member states to stop selling weapons to South Africa. This was the UN’s most significant direct action against apartheid. South Africa responded by developing its own arms industry (Armscor) and seeking covert supplies, but the embargo nonetheless damaged its military capacity.

Corporate Disinvestment and the Campaign in Universities

Beyond government sanctions, the disinvestment campaign targeted private companies. Barclays Bank — which had a major presence in South Africa through its subsidiary Barclays National Bank — faced sustained protests in British universities during the late 1970s and early 1980s. Students union campaigns against Barclays culminated in the bank selling its South African subsidiary in 1986. Shell, IBM and dozens of other corporations came under similar pressure from shareholders and consumers to divest from South Africa. By 1987, over 200 American companies had withdrawn investments.

The Commonwealth Eminent Persons Group (EPG) visited South Africa in 1986 to explore whether conditions for negotiation existed. The EPG recommended comprehensive Commonwealth sanctions after the South African government launched military raids into Zambia, Zimbabwe and Botswana — frontline states supporting the ANC — during the very week the EPG was visiting. Only Thatcher’s Britain blocked full Commonwealth sanctions, but the political isolation was already overwhelming.
exam_tip_html: When answering questions about international pressure, be specific about which form of pressure you are discussing and give precise dates. Examiners notice vague answers like “there were sanctions” — a stronger answer names the Chase Manhattan Bank crisis (1985), the US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act (1986) and the UN arms embargo (1977) separately. Also be ready to evaluate: historians debate whether sanctions caused the regime to change, or whether internal resistance was more important. Acknowledge this debate.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • International pressure on apartheid grew through sports boycotts, economic sanctions and diplomatic isolation, combining to create a financial and political crisis for the regime by the mid-1980s.
  • The Chase Manhattan Bank’s refusal to roll over South Africa’s loans in 1985 and the US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act of 1986 were the most damaging economic blows from outside the country.
  • Oliver Tambo’s ANC in exile and Desmond Tutu inside South Africa were the key figures channelling international solidarity; Reagan and Thatcher’s “constructive engagement” remained a contested alternative strategy.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the international sports boycott of apartheid South Africa.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the sports boycott AND gives a precise feature, e.g. South Africa was excluded from the Olympics from 1964; or the Gleneagles Agreement (1977) committed Commonwealth governments to discouraging sporting links. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to sports isolation. Emerging: Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the economic pressure placed on apartheid South Africa during the 1980s.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks per feature. Mastering: Two precise features — e.g. (1) Chase Manhattan Bank refused to roll over South Africa's loans in 1985, triggering a debt crisis; (2) the US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act (1986) imposed sweeping sanctions over Reagan's veto. Secure: Two features identified, one with clear detail. Developing: Two features with limited detail. Emerging: One feature or very general response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why international pressure on apartheid South Africa increased significantly during the 1980s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) the State of Emergency and township revolt made the regime's brutality visible to global television audiences; (2) the Soweto uprising and Biko's death in 1977 had already created momentum for stronger action; (3) the ANC's external mission under Tambo successfully lobbied Western governments and the UN. Each reason with specific evidence. Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Reagan and Thatcher opposed comprehensive sanctions against South Africa.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) 'constructive engagement' argument that economic ties would encourage gradual reform; (2) Cold War strategic concerns that sanctions would push South Africa towards instability that could benefit the Soviet Union. Present these as stated rationales that were contested, not as settled truths. Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-explained reason. Emerging: Vague or one-sided answer.

practice_questions.text: Outline the different forms of international pressure placed on apartheid South Africa between 1960 and 1990.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more distinct forms — sports boycotts; UN arms embargo 1977; diplomatic expulsion from Commonwealth 1961; banking sanctions (Chase Manhattan 1985); US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act 1986; corporate disinvestment. Secure: Two or three forms with some supporting detail. Developing: One or two forms. Emerging: Very general response.

practice_questions.text: How far was international pressure the most important factor in forcing the apartheid government to negotiate in the late 1980s? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing international pressure (sanctions, Chase Manhattan, Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act) against internal factors (UDF, State of Emergency, township revolt, Inkatha violence, economic costs of total strategy); reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Descriptive coverage of sanctions with limited weighing against other factors. Emerging: Narrative description.

glossary_terms.definition: The international movement, centred on the UK organisation founded in 1959, campaigning for economic and cultural boycotts to pressure South Africa to end apartheid.
Anglican priest and campaigner who co-founded the British Anti-Apartheid Movement in 1959 and spent decades working for South Africa's liberation.
A 1977 agreement by Commonwealth heads of government to discourage sporting links with South Africa, following controversy over New Zealand's rugby tour.
The New York bank that, in August 1985, refused to roll over South Africa's short-term debt, triggering a financial crisis and forcing the South African government to declare a debt moratorium.
A 1986 US law imposing comprehensive economic sanctions on South Africa, passed by Congress over President Reagan's veto.

ANC president leading the external mission from Lusaka; his diplomatic skill was crucial in winning international support for sanctions and keeping the ANC recognised as the legitimate liberation movement.
Anglican Archbishop of Cape Town from 1986; a Nobel Peace Prize winner who used his moral authority to campaign for sanctions and for a negotiated, peaceful end to apartheid.

The group of Commonwealth leaders who visited South Africa in 1986 to assess the possibility of negotiations; their report strongly backed sanctions after the South African government refused to engage meaningfully.
